Avoid `as TypeName` type assertions for type narrowing; at runtime, prefer `instanceof` checks and throw a descriptive `Error` (e.g., pointing to the project issue tracker) when the expected type is not satisfied. Avoid `// @ts-ignore`; when a TypeScript type error is genuinely unavoidable (e.g., a known gap in a third-party library's types such as Jison), use `// @ts-expect-error: <descriptive reason>` instead. Never place a file-level `@ts-ignore` or `@ts-expect-error` directive to suppress all TypeScript errors across an entire module; add suppression comments only to the specific lines that require them.
Diagram definition objects should omit optional properties that are not yet implemented (e.g., `styles`) rather than including them with empty arrays or undefined values.
TypeScript source files in this project use lowercase filenames (e.g., `interfaces.ts`, `baseAxis.ts`); do not use PascalCase filenames such as `Interfaces.ts` or `BaseAxis.ts`.

TypeScript interface and type alias names must not be prefixed with `I` (e.g., use `TextDimensionCalculator`, not `ITextDimensionCalculator`); the project does not follow the Hungarian `I`-prefix convention. Prefer deriving complex types with `typeof` or mapped types rather than manually writing parallel interface declarations.

Prefer early `return`/`continue`/`throw` statements over deeply nested if-else chains. When an `if` block returns or throws early, remove the subsequent `else` block — it is structurally unnecessary and adds indentation noise. When an `if` branch tests a negated condition, consider swapping the if and else branches so the affirmative case appears first. When a conditional branch always throws, subsequent conditions should use plain `if` statements rather than `else if`.

In all mermaid diagram examples (demos, documentation, Cypress integration tests, and test fixtures), use the frontmatter configuration block (a `---` YAML header) to set diagram config. The older directives syntax (`%%{init: ...}%%`) is considered obsolete in this project and should not be introduced in new or updated examples. When documenting configuration options, show only the YAML frontmatter block as the example — do not include a sample diagram body in the config snippet.

In diagram rendering and utility code, use the project's structured logger (`log.debug()`, `log.trace()`, etc. from `packages/mermaid/src/logger.ts`) rather than `console.log`, `console.warn`, or any other `console.*` methods. Use `log.debug()` or `log.trace()` for development debugging statements rather than `log.info()` or `log.warn()`. Remove all `console.*` statements and excessively chatty or unnecessary debug/trace logging before merging; keep only meaningful diagnostic logs.
Method and function names in TypeScript must fully spell out words without abbreviations or typos (e.g., `getDrawableElementsForBottomAxis`, not `getDrawableElemsForBottomAxes`).

In tests, prefer direct indexed assertions (`expect(array[0].property).toBe(...)`) over `.forEach()` loops or `for`/`switch` dispatches when asserting on specific elements. Direct assertions produce more targeted failure messages and are easier to read as documentation of expected behavior.

When adding links to GitHub Issues in project documentation, consolidate open and closed issue searches into a single link using the `?q=is%3Aissue` query parameter (e.g., `https://github.com/mermaid-js/mermaid/issues?q=is%3Aissue`) and label it to indicate it covers both states.

Prefer template literals (backtick strings with `${}` interpolation) over string concatenation with `+` for all dynamic string construction in both source and test files — especially for SVG attribute values like `transform`, error messages, and log strings. When the interpolated value is a non-primitive (e.g., a `[number, number]` array from a D3 centroid), use an explicit conversion such as `.join(', ')` or `.toString()` rather than relying on implicit coercion, so the resulting string format is intentional and clear.

Test descriptions (`it`/`test` strings) should explicitly name the specific function or public API being exercised, not just describe the behavior in generic terms. For example, prefer 'should clean up comments inside `getDiagramFromText` when present in diagram definition' over 'should clean up comments when present in diagram definition', so the unit under test is immediately clear without reading the test body.
Use two-space indentation throughout `.langium` grammar files, consistent with the project's Langium formatting convention.
Use strict equality operators (`===` / `!==`) instead of loose equality (`==` / `!=`) throughout TypeScript and JavaScript source files.

Do not insert blank lines between import statements within an import block; blank lines within import blocks can interfere with auto-sort tooling and create noisy diffs. Keep all imports from the same library or package in a single `import` statement rather than splitting them across multiple statements.

New helper, utility, and diagram implementation files added to the project must use the `.ts` extension and be fully typed rather than being added as `.js` files; TypeScript types improve maintainability and catch errors at compile time.
Throw errors directly with `throw new Error(...)` rather than first assigning the error to a local variable when that variable serves no purpose other than to be thrown on the very next line.

In xychart spec and parser test files, format multi-line diagram strings inside template literals with minimal, consistent indentation (ideally flush to the left margin or a single shallow indent level) so the diagram syntax is human-readable without visually misleading extra whitespace.

When iterating over a collection to call a single-parameter diagram database method, prefer a direct function reference (e.g., `ast.sections.map(db.addSection)`) over an arrow-function wrapper (e.g., `ast.sections.map((s) => db.addSection(s))`), provided the method accepts exactly one argument.

Do not include unrelated whitespace, indentation, formatting, or import reordering changes in a feature PR; revert them or move them to a separate dedicated clean-up PR so the diff remains focused on the stated change.

When extracting substrings from regular expression matches, use named capture groups (`(?<name>pattern)`) and reference them via `.groups.name` rather than positional numeric indices (e.g., `match[1]`). This applies throughout `ganttDb.js` and any other file that uses regex to parse diagram syntax.

Use the semantic `<kbd>` HTML element to mark up keyboard key names in user-facing UI text (hints, labels, tooltips) rather than plain `<span>` tags or bare text. For example: `<kbd>{{ ctrlSymbol }}</kbd> + <kbd>Enter</kbd>`. This conveys correct semantics and accessibility meaning.
Prefer `interface` over `type` aliases for TypeScript type definitions; this convention is enforced by the `@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-definitions` ESLint rule configured in `.eslintrc.cjs`.

Type local variables used as string-keyed dictionaries with an explicit `Record<KeyType, ValueType>` annotation (e.g., `const links: Record<string, string> = {}`) rather than leaving them as inferred `{}` or `object`.

In Cypress `imgSnapshotTest` calls using template literals, ensure the closing backtick and closing parenthesis are each on their own correctly-indented line; misplaced closures cause subtle syntax or argument-passing bugs.

Provide explicit type annotations on class field declarations, especially when the field is initialized with an empty object or array literal (`= {}`), so the intended shape is unambiguous without requiring inference.
Prefer `for...of` loops over `.forEach()` for array iteration; this reduces nesting, is idiomatic TypeScript, and is the preferred style in this project.

Within a single test file, be consistent about whether Map keys are iterated in sorted order (`[...map.keys()].sort()`) or natural insertion order (`[...map.keys()]`); do not mix approaches without a documented reason.

In test snapshot assertions for HTML-rendering utilities (e.g., `handle-markdown-text.spec.ts`), represent non-breaking spaces as the explicit HTML entity ` ` rather than the invisible Unicode U+00A0 character. Using the HTML entity keeps expected values human-readable, stays consistent with other assertions in the same file, and avoids needing `/* eslint-disable no-irregular-whitespace */` suppression comments.

Use `Map` instead of plain objects (`{}`) for all dictionary/lookup data structures in rendering utilities (e.g., `mermaid-graphlib.js`, `clusters.js`); this is an established project-wide convention.

Mermaid-defined config option string literals should use camelCase (e.g., `'handDrawn'`, `'classic'`); UPPER_SNAKE_CASE is reserved for string values that directly map to external library constants (e.g., ELK strategy names such as `'NETWORK_SIMPLEX'`, `'BRANDES_KOEPF'`).

Apply consistent camelCase in TypeScript identifiers: capitalize acronyms and initialisms fully (e.g., `getID` not `getId`), and rename any leftover `snake_case` or inconsistently-cased variables encountered in the same refactoring pass.
In V11+ error objects, omit placeholder `loc`, `line`, and `token` fields from error hashes rather than filling them with dummy values.

Prefer TypeScript's implicit type inference over explicit type annotations when the type is unambiguous from context (e.g., `const x = getConfig()` rather than `const x: MermaidConfig = getConfig()`); avoid redundant annotations on locally-inferred `const` variables. Explicit annotations remain required when the inferred type would be incorrect or too narrow (e.g., `let` variables initialized to `null`).
When constructing an object literal that must conform to an interface (e.g., `Commit`), use the `satisfies` keyword to get type-checking without widening the inferred type.
Within a module file, order declarations as: type and interface definitions first, then `const` declarations, then `let` declarations.

Define enum-like constant objects with `as const` so values are inferred as literal types; give the constant a name that clearly communicates it is a map of all variants rather than a single variant; define it in exactly one place and import it wherever needed, avoiding duplicate definitions.
In TypeScript interface and type definitions, list required properties before optional (`?`) ones.
Mark optional function parameters with the `?` modifier rather than including `| undefined` in a union type.
Remove inline comments that merely restate what the code already expresses; keep only comments that explain non-obvious intent, constraints, or context.

When creating spies with `vi.spyOn`, name the variable to reflect both the target object and the method being observed, suffixed with `Spy` (e.g., `logWarnSpy` for `vi.spyOn(log, 'warn')`). Avoid generic names like `spy` or the bare method name, which make it harder to understand the spy's scope at a glance.

In `.changeset/*.md` files: (a) use lowercase for the bump type (`patch`, `minor`, `major` — not `Patch` etc.; incorrect casing causes changeset processing to fail); (b) conventional commit type prefixes (`fix:`, `feat:`, `chore:`) must be followed by a space before the description text (e.g., `fix: description`, not `fix:description`); (c) capitalize the first word of the description that follows the type prefix (e.g., `feat: Add ...` not `feat: add ...`).

When suppressing ESLint warnings with `// eslint-disable` comments, disable only the specific rule(s) responsible (e.g., `// eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any`) rather than using blanket suppressions that silence all rules for a line or block.
